title: Laws of Combination of Resistances
short_intro: Combination of resistances involves joining multiple resistors in series or parallel configurations to achieve a desired equivalent resistance in an electrical circuit. The equivalent resistance depends strictly on the topological arrangement and obeys Ohm's Law.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Calculation of equivalent resistance for simple series, parallel, and symmetrical bridge networks; basic application of Ohm's Law and Kirchhoff's Rules.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Infinite ladder networks, delta-wstar (triangle-star) transformations, complex symmetry in cubical or planar resistor networks, and temperature dependence of resistance combinations.

prerequisites: Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) and Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL)
Conservation of charge and energy in circuits

concept_notes.heading: Series Combination of Resistors
bullets: Resistors are connected end-to-end such that the same electric current flows through each resistor sequentially.
The total potential difference across the combination is equal to the sum of the potential drops across individual resistors: V = V<sub>1</sub> + V<sub>2</sub> + ... + V<sub>n</sub>.
The equivalent resistance R<sub>s</sub> is always greater than the largest individual resistance in the combination.

concept_notes.heading: Parallel Combination of Resistors
bullets: Resistors are connected across the same two common nodes, ensuring the same potential difference exists across each resistor.
The total current entering the parallel junction divides among the branches such that I = I<sub>1</sub> + I<sub>2</sub> + ... + I<sub>n</sub>.
The reciprocal of the equivalent resistance R<sub>p</sub> equals the sum of the reciprocals of individual resistances, making R<sub>p</sub> smaller than the smallest individual resistor.

concept_notes.heading: Delta-Star (Triangle-Wye) Transformation
bullets: Used for analyzing bridge circuits that cannot be simplified purely by standard series or parallel combinations.
Converts a three-terminal delta (mesh) connection of resistances into an equivalent star (tee) connection.
Simplifies complex network analysis by eliminating bridge cross-connections.

concept_notes.heading: Symmetry in Resistor Networks
bullets: Mirror symmetry and perpendicular axis symmetry allow identification of equipotential nodes where no current flows.
Unneeded branches connected between equipotential nodes can be removed to simplify complex configurations like a cube resistance network.
Reduces computational complexity in advanced PGT numerical problems.

derivations.title: Equivalent Resistance in Series Combination
derivations.conditions: n resistors connected sequentially carrying identical current I
steps: Let n resistors R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub>, ..., R<sub>n</sub> be connected in series across a voltage source V.
By Ohm's Law, the potential drop across each resistor is V<sub>i</sub> = I R<sub>i</sub>.
The total potential difference is V = V<sub>1</sub> + V<sub>2</sub> + ... + V<sub>n</sub> = I(R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>2</sub> + ... + R<sub>n</sub>).
Defining equivalent resistance R<sub>s</sub> as V / I yields the final expression.

derivations.title: Equivalent Resistance in Parallel Combination
derivations.conditions: n resistors connected across common nodes with identical potential difference V
steps: Let n resistors R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub>, ..., R<sub>n</sub> be connected in parallel across voltage V.
The current through each branch is given by I<sub>i</sub> = V / R<sub>i</sub>.
Total current entering the junction is I = I<sub>1</sub> + I<sub>2</sub> + ... + I<sub>n</sub> = V(1/R<sub>1</sub> + 1/R<sub>2</sub> + ... + 1/R<sub>n</sub>).
Using equivalent resistance R<sub>p</sub> where I = V / R<sub>p</sub> gives the reciprocal relation.

graphs_and_experiments.title: V-I Characteristics for Series and Parallel Combinations
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A graph of Current (I) on the x-axis versus Potential Difference (V) on the y-axis, showing straight lines with different slopes for series and parallel circuits.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the V-I graph represents the equivalent resistance (R = V/I). A steeper slope indicates a higher equivalent resistance (series combination), whereas a shallower slope indicates a lower equivalent resistance (parallel combination).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in conceptual multiple-choice questions comparing slopes of series and parallel configurations.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Metre Bridge Experiment for Resistance Combination Verification
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Circuit diagram of a Metre Bridge connected to a resistance box and unknown resistors in series/parallel configurations with a galvanometer and jockey.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: At the null point, the ratio of lengths (l/(100-l)) equals the ratio of resistances, allowing experimental verification of R<sub>s<sub> and R<sub>p<sub> formulas.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in practical physics applications and numerical problems based on null-deflection balancing length.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Infinite Resistance Ladder Network
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An infinite repeating ladder network of alternating series and parallel resistors connected across input terminals.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Due to infinite repetition, removing one repeating unit leaves the input equivalent resistance unchanged, setting up a quadratic equation for R<sub>eq<sub>.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Advanced PGT examination problem type assessing asymptotic network analysis.

solved_numericals.question: Three resistors of resistances 2 Ω, 3 Ω, and 6 Ω are connected in parallel. Calculate the equivalent resistance of the combination.
solution_steps: Recall the formula for parallel combination: 1/R_p = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + 1/R_3.
Invert to find R_p: R_p = 1 Ω.

solved_numericals.question: A wire of resistance R is cut into 5 equal pieces. If these pieces are connected in parallel, find the equivalent resistance of the combination in terms of R.
solution_steps: When a wire is cut into 5 equal parts, the resistance of each individual piece becomes R' = R / 5.
When n identical resistors of value R' are connected in parallel, the equivalent resistance is R_p = R' / n.
Substitute R' = R / 5 and n = 5: R_p = (R / 5) / 5 = R / 25.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the equivalent resistance between terminals A and B of a cube skeleton where each edge has a resistance r.
solution_steps: Apply symmetry principles to the cubical network connected between diagonally opposite corners (A and B).
Current entering node A divides symmetrically into 3 edges, each carrying current I/3. The potential at these three nodes is equal.
At the next set of 3 symmetric nodes, current recombines symmetrically before exiting at node B.
Sum the potential drops along a path from A to B: V_AB = (1/3)r + (1/6)r + (1/3)r = (5/6)r.

assumptions_and_limitations: Resistors are assumed to be ohmic, meaning their resistance remains constant irrespective of the current or applied voltage.
Connecting wires and terminal contacts are assumed to have zero electrical resistance unless explicitly stated otherwise.
Temperature variations during current flow are neglected in basic combination laws (Temperature coefficient of resistance alpha is taken as zero).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Adding resistors in parallel increases the total equivalent resistance of the circuit.
common_misconceptions.correct: Adding resistors in parallel decreases the equivalent resistance.
common_misconceptions.why: Parallel connection provides additional alternate conducting paths for current, lowering the overall obstruction to flow.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The current is divided equally among all resistors in a parallel combination regardless of their resistance values.
common_misconceptions.correct: Current divides inversely proportional to the resistance of each branch.
common_misconceptions.why: Branches with smaller resistance carry larger currents according to Ohm's Law (I = V/R).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Connecting identical resistors in series increases the current drawn from a fixed voltage source.
common_misconceptions.correct: Connecting resistors in series increases total resistance, thereby decreasing the total current drawn from the source.
common_misconceptions.why: From Ohm's Law, current is inversely proportional to total series resistance (I = V / nR).

quick_revision: Series combination maximizes equivalent resistance (R_s = Σ R_i), whereas parallel combination minimizes it (1/R_p = Σ 1/R_i).
Series Equivalent Resistance: R_{s} = R_{1} + R_{2} + R_{3} + ... + R_{n}
